methods.text: Fix the order of steps before designing any single step.
Mark every number with where it came from.
Make the same piece with half the parts.
Start from the step users skip most often.
List what changes when the numbers double, and design for that.
Put the most common answer where the eye lands first.
Keep a log of every decision and its reason, then reread it at the end.
Build the part users touch most before anything else.

constraints.text: Every input states its allowed range next to it.
Rounds every result to at most two decimal places.

tasks.text: Churn cost calculator: customers, the share lost each month, and value per customer give revenue lost per year and what one point less churn would save.
Price change tester: current price, volume, and an expected change in volume give revenue and margin at five price points, side by side.
Rework cost tally: cases per month, error rate, and cost to fix each give the monthly cost of rework and the saving at a lower error rate.
Tool overlap finder: the buyer's current tools with cost and uses give the functions covered twice and the yearly spend on duplicates.
Handoff wait check: the points where work passes between people or teams, with wait times, give the number of handoffs and the longest wait.
Budget-to-scope sheet: a budget and a list of wanted features with rough costs give which features fit, in priority order, and what is left over.

guests.text: historical | Gregor Mendel | Count the results of many small trials before stating a rule. | died 1884
literary | Phileas Fogg | Plan every leg against the clock and keep a margin for delays. | Jules Verne, died 1905

temperaments.text: Repeats the other side's point back before answering.
Asks what it would cost to be wrong.
Waits until everyone has spoken, then sums up.
Brings a checklist and works through it in order.

guests: historical | Euclid | State a few assumptions, then build everything from them. | died c. 270 BC
historical | Ibn al-Haytham | Trust nothing until an experiment shows it. | died c. 1040
temperaments: Agrees fast, then quietly does it their own way.
Argues the opposite side to test an idea.
methods: Design the error and empty states first.
List the assumptions in the brief and check each one.
Make it work in black and white before adding color.
Take the conventions of a genre and break exactly one.
Write the copy before the layout.
Scope the work to what fits in one day.
constraints: Under 100 words of fixed text on the page.
tasks: Cost-of-inaction calculator: the buyer's current volumes and rates give what the problem costs per month and per year, with each step of the sum shown.
Readiness scorecard: twelve yes-or-no questions give a score out of 100, the three weakest areas, and one next step for each.
Benchmark checker: the buyer's own figures sit next to typical ranges they can edit, with each gap marked ahead, level, or behind.
Leak finder: a funnel of stages with counts gives the stage that loses the most and what fixing half of that loss would be worth.
Time-back calculator: weekly hours on manual tasks and an hourly cost give the hours and money an automated step would return.
Before-and-after map: today's process as a list of steps becomes a side-by-side view marking the steps that could be removed or automated.
